
SHEET Charts
B40: Only severe memory pressure is what caused jobs to be missed. Seeing as the baseline program expended about 1.3 GB of RAM, the extra 2 MB made
B41: it difficult to schedule all of the jobs on time. However, while this happened on one of the runs, we cannot say with certainty that ths is not an outlier
B42: because in the other 2 trials, even with the added memory pressure, all of the jobs were able to complete. More trials would have to be run, but the overall premise is sound that memory pressure will eventually cause jobs to be missed.
B78: The median response time seems to have no identifiable difference other than when the process is scheduled to the lowest possible priority. We would
B79: imagine that in a real implementation of the critter that sampling and reporting would be the highest priority processes, and even when the process is in
B80: the middle of the pack priority wise, it still meets timing requirements. So the critter only does not meet timing if it is absolutely last in priority. 
B116: Memory pressure has a slight affect on schedulign with 2 and 1.5 GiB producing slightly higher response times, but scheduling really has the largest effect.
B117: When the taks is a lower priority, it is subject to much larger outliers in this category that certainly advocate for processes like sampling for the critter being 
B118: put as the highest priority.
B154: As there is barely any data to support this and only one trial, we can see that the wait time as compared to the completion time is massive, and we can only
B155: really use this as a cautionary tale to to ensure that we never miss a deadline as there can be a long time to wait before we begin meeting deadlines again.
B192: The maximum acquisition gap is also susceptible to memory pressure as well as being assigned a low-priority process. However, the increase for lower
B193: priority processes is very minimal - it is a cautionary tale that memroy pressure simply makes maximum acquisition gap outliers possible.
B230: Again, this metric really only serves as a warning as to make sure that there is no missed deadlines as the sequences can be very long before deadlines
B231: are met again.
B235: What this means for the Critter
B236: This means for the critter that as long as the program executes sequentially in the implementation that we have right now, that it will be able to successfully
B237: meet deadlines with just one core and with a power saving speed governor. Further testing will have to be performed to see if each of these experiments 
B238: compound. For now however, we can be confident that the critter implementation will be reliable one one core and may even be possible to network
B239: in the case that we hagve more than one critter for large HVAC appliations.
B241: What this means for embedded systems as a whole
B242: For this particular experiment, we do not have to worry about the slight variations and noise that we see because we do not have hard real-time requirements.
B243: In cases where the real-time requirements are hard, we would need to perform significant expeirmentation in thje environment to make sure that all 
B244: deadlines are met even in cases where the environment may be extreme. For cases such as a pacemaker that may require a bluetooth connection, this 
B245: research can help support that one core may be sufficient for the entire workload of transmitting data to a bluetooth application if the thread that senses
B246: and provides electrical stimulus has a higher priority. Although, the most dangerous piece of evidence here seems to be the memory pressure. 
B247: In cases where data accumulates and eats up too much of ram, that is where we begin to see the unacceptable levels of delays and missed deadlines. 
B248: This is where it ties back into code safety and why we cannot be allocating memory after initialization for these extremely critical applications, because
B249: in cases where programs fail and data accumulates and eats up too much memory, that is when we will see these incredibly expensive deadline misses.
